title: What the Pear Tree Knew
text: The pear tree at the far end of Grandad’s allotment was older than my mother, and it carried its age with an air of quiet superiority. The pear stood apart from the fussing apple trees, gnarled and unhurried, its branches twisted like the knuckles of an old hand, and I had spent most Saturdays of my childhood beneath it.

This autumn, for the first time, I went alone. Grandad had moved in the summer to a ground-floor flat, where his stiff knees no longer had to contend with the steep path, and before he left he had pressed the shed key into my hand with the solemnity of a man handing over a crown. “Somebody ought to see to the pears,” he had said, gazing out of the window rather than at me, as though the request had cost him a good deal more than he intended to admit.

The fruit was ready; I could tell because the air beneath the branches hung thick and sweet, and the wasps, drunk on sugar, drifted through it without the slightest interest in me. I hauled the tall ladder into place and began to pick, easing each pear from its stalk with a small, reluctant twist. By noon six crates stood in a row.

What I had not anticipated was how much of Grandad I would find in the work. With every branch I reached, I heard his instructions: never pull, always twist; leave the small ones, since they are still deciding. His advice had always arrived sideways, folded inside stories about his own father, who had grown this tree from a pip and been laughed at by every plot-holder on the row. “Pears take their time,” Grandad would say. “A decade before the first fruit, and most people haven’t the patience.” It had not occurred to me until that afternoon that he might not have been talking about pears.

By late afternoon I faced a difficulty, because six crates were far more than one family could eat. I might have sold them at the gate, as the neighbouring plot-holders did, but I thought instead of Mrs Okafor, who had once left a jar of chutney on our shed step without so much as a note, and of the young couple with twins, who never seemed to own a spare minute between them. I began to carry pears down the path, one paper bag at a time.

Dusk was gathering by the time I reached Grandad’s flat with the last bag cradled against my chest. He was in his armchair, and when I laid a single pear in his palm he turned it over, pressed his thumb beside the stalk, and smiled slowly, as though it were a letter from someone he had missed.
“You twisted them,” he said. It was not a question.
“I did.”
“And the small ones?”
“Still deciding.”

He laughed, a dry, delighted laugh, and bit into the fruit; juice ran down his chin. Somewhere between the ladder and the armchair I had understood that the tree had never been about pears at all. It concerned what a person leaves for others, and how long they are willing to wait for it.

title: Bogs That Breathe
text: When most people imagine a threatened habitat, they picture a rainforest or a coral reef. Few think of a bog. Yet the soggy, spongy landscapes known as peatlands are among the most valuable places on Earth, and in many countries, including the United Kingdom, they are quietly disappearing.

A peat bog begins with water that cannot drain away. In waterlogged ground, dead plants do not rot in the usual way, because rotting depends on tiny living things that need air, and there is very little air in sodden soil. Instead, the remains of plants, especially mosses, pile up layer upon layer and are slowly squashed into a dark, crumbly material called peat. The process is extraordinarily slow: a bog may grow by only about a millimetre a year. The deepest peat in Britain began to form thousands of years ago.

This matters because plants take in carbon dioxide from the air as they grow. When plants rot, most of that carbon returns to the atmosphere. In a bog, however, it stays locked in the peat. Although peatlands cover only about three per cent of the world’s land, they hold more carbon than all of the world’s forests put together. Scientists sometimes describe them as a vast natural storeroom for carbon.

The trouble begins when bogs are drained. For centuries, people have dug peat to burn as fuel, drained the land to create farms, or sold the peat as compost for gardens. Once a bog dries out, air reaches the peat, and the rotting that was paused for thousands of years begins again. The stored carbon escapes as carbon dioxide, and a bog that once helped to keep the planet cooler starts to warm it instead.

Bogs matter for other reasons too. Their mosses soak up rainwater like enormous sponges, which slows the flow of water into rivers and can reduce flooding in towns downstream. Rare wildlife lives in them: dragonflies breed in the bog pools, and a small plant called the sundew traps insects on sticky, glistening hairs to gain the nutrients that the poor, acidic soil cannot provide. Because peat contains so little air, it can also preserve ancient wooden objects for centuries, so bogs are valued by people who study the past.

The encouraging news is that some of the damage can be reversed. Conservation teams block the ditches that drain a bog, building small dams from wood, plastic or peat, so that water backs up and the ground grows wet again. Volunteers then plant clumps of sphagnum moss, the main peat-forming plant, and within a few years the bare, cracked surface begins to turn green. Many gardeners now choose peat-free compost, which reduces the demand for digging bogs up.

Restoring a bog requires patience. Nobody can rebuild in an afternoon what nature took thousands of years to make. Even so, each wet, mossy field that is brought back to life is a step in the right direction, because a healthy bog does its work quietly, day after day, without anyone noticing.

title: A Piece Out of Place
text: On Thursday afternoon the chess club at Larkhill Primary made a startling discovery: the white queen had vanished. Mr Adeyemi, who ran the club, held the wooden box open, and the empty velvet hollow gaped at the children like a missing tooth. “Every piece was here at lunchtime,” he said, his voice unusually tight, “and I counted them myself, so with the tournament tomorrow we have a serious problem: nobody can play without a queen.”

Eleven children stood around the table, each wearing an expression of studied innocence. Hana, who read detective stories by torchlight under her duvet, said nothing at all, for she maintained that the truth was rarely hidden and was merely waiting for someone patient enough to notice it.

“Who had the box last?” she asked eventually, but nobody could say, for the box had lived in the cupboard in Room 6 since lunch and the only key hung on a hook behind Mr Adeyemi’s desk. Yet the cupboard door, Hana observed, stood open by the width of a finger, and when she crouched she saw on the carpet a single glittering speck of silver, while the air near the shelf carried a faint, sharp smell that she could not immediately place.
“Perhaps somebody took it as a joke,” muttered Ewan, folding his arms. “Or as a strategy,” retorted Priya, glaring at him, “since some people would do almost anything to avoid playing me.”

Hana ignored them both, because she was watching Callum. He stood at the edge of the group with his hands buried in his sleeves, which in itself was unremarkable, since Callum was shy and habitually hovered on the fringes of things. What held her attention was the restless movement of his fingertips inside the cuffs, which pressed together and then parted with a tiny, reluctant tug, as though something tacky were clinging to them. She thought again about the smell: sharp, chemical, faintly sweet. It belonged in the art room, beside the trays of glitter, and it belonged to glue.

Hana asked whether anyone had used the room after lunch, and Mr Adeyemi answered that only Callum had, since he had stayed behind to stack the chairs; every head turned, and Callum’s face flushed the colour of beetroot.
Hana stepped closer and lowered her voice so that only he could hear. “I don’t think you took it,” she said. “I think you mended it.”

For a long moment Callum studied the floor. Then, slowly, he drew the white queen from his blazer pocket. A jagged crack ran through her crown, sealed with a bead of glue, and a dusting of silver glitter clung to her base. “I knocked the box off the table,” he whispered. “Her crown snapped off, and I was too embarrassed to say, so I took her to the art room. I only wanted to fix her before anyone found out.”

Mr Adeyemi turned the piece over in his palm, and his frown dissolved. “A little glue between friends,” he said. “I can think of far worse crimes.” Callum gave a shaky laugh, and Hana, smiling, set the queen on the radiator to dry.

title: Should Museums Be Free?
text: Every year, millions of people walk through the doors of museums to admire dinosaur skeletons, ancient jewellery and paintings hundreds of years old. In some places, entry costs nothing; in others, visitors must pay at the desk. Should museums be free for everyone, or is it fair to charge?

Those who believe in free entry begin with fairness. Museums look after objects that belong, in a sense, to everybody, and it seems wrong that a family with little money should be shut out of its own history. A single ticket may seem cheap to one person, but for a family of five the cost can mount up quickly. When entry is free, children who would never otherwise visit can wander in on a wet afternoon, and a lifelong curiosity may begin with a single glance at a fossil.

Supporters also point out that free museums encourage short, relaxed visits. Someone can spend twenty minutes studying one painting and return next week to see another, rather than feeling obliged to squeeze in everything to justify the price of a ticket. Free museums can also bring life to the streets around them, since visitors often stop at nearby cafés and shops.

Those who favour charging offer a different argument. Museums are expensive to run. Fragile objects must be kept at the right temperature, guarded, cleaned and repaired by trained experts, and the buildings themselves need heating, lighting and repairs. If governments or councils cannot provide enough money, the museum must earn it elsewhere, and ticket sales are one of the most reliable ways of doing so.

They also argue that a small fee can be fair if it is paid only by people who choose to visit. Taxpayers who never set foot in a museum still help to fund a free one; charging moves part of the cost to those who enjoy it. Some museums have found a compromise. They keep their main galleries free but charge for special exhibitions, or they invite visitors to give whatever they can afford as they leave.

Each side has an answer to the other. Critics of charging say that even a suggested donation can make people feel awkward if they have little to give. Critics of free entry reply that donations rarely cover the full cost of keeping a museum open and that the quality of its collections may suffer.

In the end, both sides want much the same thing: for museums to survive, and for as many people as possible to enjoy them. The real disagreement is about who should pay. Perhaps each community must decide for itself how to balance the fairness of open doors against the practical cost of keeping them open. Readers may wish to weigh up the arguments and reach a view of their own.

title: The Apprentice’s First Sheet
text: Haru had been Master Sato’s apprentice for nearly a year, and in all that time he had never once been permitted to make a sheet of paper. Instead he carried water, stripped the bark from bundles of branches until his fingers cracked, and swept a workshop floor that was already spotless, all the while wondering whether he would ever prove worthy of the craft for which the village of Yamane, folded into a valley of tall cedars, was renowned.

Winter arrived early that year. Frost furred the roofs, and the river that ran past the workshop was so cold that it made his wrists ache, yet Master Sato insisted that this was the finest season for the work, since the cold kept the fibres pure and the water clean. “Cold water is honest,” he liked to say. “It hides nothing.”

On the first morning of the new year, the old man placed in Haru’s hands a wooden frame with a bamboo screen stretched across it. “Today you will make paper,” he said, and Haru’s heart leapt as he dipped the frame into the great vat, where pale pulp drifted in water made slippery by the juice of a plant root, and lifted it out, rocking it forward and back exactly as he had watched it done for months.

The sheet that resulted was a disaster: thick as felt in one corner, and so thin in another that daylight shone through it like a window. Haru’s face burned. “It is ruined,” he said. “I am sorry, Master.” Master Sato made no reply. He peeled the damp sheet from the screen, laid it on a board and handed back the frame, and Haru made a second sheet, then a third, then a tenth, his arms trembling and the cold gnawing at his fingers. By afternoon his sheets were less ragged, and by evening a few were almost even, though none resembled the smooth, silky paper that stacked the shelves.

When the lamps were lit, the old man carried the day’s pile to the drying boards and smoothed each sheet flat with a soft brush. Only one did he lift to the glow of the lantern: the very first, with its heavy corner and its see-through one. “Look,” he said. “The light passes through here and stops there. This is the only sheet that shows me what you were thinking.” Haru frowned; he had assumed it would be the first to be thrown away.

“Every sheet you make from now on will be better,” said Master Sato, “but that is the easy part. The hard part is remembering how it felt to be bad at it.” Then he slid the paper into a wooden drawer, where Haru glimpsed other sheets already yellowed with age, each of them with a crooked corner. “My master kept mine,” said the old man, and he blew out the lamp.

title: Letters Cast in Metal
text: Before the middle of the fifteenth century, every book in Europe had to be copied out by hand. Scribes, most of them monks, sat for months at a time bent over a single volume, dipping their pens and forming each letter with painstaking care. The results could be beautiful, but they were so slow to produce and so costly to buy that only churches, universities and wealthy families could afford more than a handful of books. For almost everybody else, reading material was scarce.

In the German city of Mainz, around 1450, a goldsmith named Johannes Gutenberg began to wonder whether there might be a quicker way. Printers of the time already carved whole pages into blocks of wood, but a block could print only the page it had been cut for, and the carving itself was laborious. Gutenberg’s insight was to make each letter separately, so that the same pieces could be arranged to form any page and then rearranged for the next.

Making such letters demanded all of his skill as a metalworker. He cut the shape of each character into a hard metal punch, pressed the punch into a softer piece of metal to form a mould, and poured a hot mixture of lead, tin and antimony into the mould, where it cooled into a small block bearing a raised, back-to-front letter. Hundreds of identical letters could be cast from a single mould, and because they were made of metal they were tough enough to be used again and again.

Gutenberg also had to find an ink that would cling to metal, since the watery ink used by scribes simply ran off. After many experiments he produced a thick, sticky ink made with oil. For the press itself he adapted a heavy wooden screw press of the kind used to squeeze juice from grapes. The letters were arranged in a frame, line by line, and inked; a sheet of paper was laid on top, and the screw was turned to press the paper down firmly. When the sheet was lifted away, the page was printed, and the same letters could be inked again at once.

Gutenberg’s greatest project was a Latin Bible, which occupied him and his workers for several years. Roughly a hundred and eighty copies were printed, each running to well over a thousand pages, and a scribe would have needed a very long time to copy even one. The work was expensive, however, and Gutenberg had borrowed heavily to pay for it. When the debt fell due, he lost his workshop, and his former partners carried on printing without him.

The idea, though, could not be stopped. Printers set up presses in one city after another, and by about 1500 there were presses in more than two hundred European towns. In 1476 William Caxton opened the first press in England, at Westminster, and began to print books in English. As books grew cheaper, more people learned to read, and news, ideas and knowledge travelled faster than they ever had before.

title: Tallest in the Tent
text: Beneath the canvas of the village show tent, where the air hung thick with the smell of trampled grass and warm tea, the judge’s pen hovered above her clipboard for what felt like an hour. Outside, a brass band competed with the shrieks of children on the bouncy castle, but Imani could hear nothing except the relentless pounding of her own pulse.

Her sunflower stood at the end of the long table, tall and brazen, its enormous face angled towards the light as though it were fully aware of being watched. She had grown it from a seed scarcely larger than her thumbnail, and every morning since April she had watered it, measured it and murmured encouragement, while her little sister, unimpressed, had rolled her eyes and enquired whether it had answered back.

Beside it stood Dev’s entry. Dev lived three doors down and had walked to school beside her for as long as either of them could remember. His sunflower was slighter, its stalk bent in a diffident curve, its head drooping a little lower than seemed dignified. When the two of them had pushed their seeds into the soil in spring, they had made a pact: whoever lost would buy the other an ice cream. It had seemed a wonderfully small thing to wager.

“Tallest sunflower,” announced the judge, unfolding a tape measure with a flourish, and she held it against Dev’s stalk first, murmuring figures under her breath. Then she moved along to Imani’s, and Imani’s stomach lurched. Concealed beneath the cloth that skirted the pot was the upturned bucket she had balanced it on at seven that morning, to stop the pot from wobbling on the uneven ground. Until this very second, it had not occurred to her what the bucket would do to the measurement.
“Two hundred and forty-two centimetres,” read the judge. “Dev’s was two hundred and thirty-eight. We have a winner.”

She pinned a red rosette beside the pot and nodded, evidently satisfied. Around her, people applauded. Imani’s mother, near the entrance, was beaming so broadly that her cheeks must have ached. Dev clapped too, a fraction late, and his smile arrived slowly, as if it had been fetched from somewhere a very long way off.

Imani felt the silk ribbons of the rosette brush her wrist. It would be so easy, she reasoned. Nobody had lied, and nobody had cheated; the judge had measured precisely what she had been shown. And yet the bucket sat beneath its cloth like a stone in a shoe, a small, hard fact that every step would only make worse. She thought of the ice cream, of the three doors, of years of walking to school, and she understood that the prize was already costing her more than it was worth.

“Excuse me,” she heard herself say. Her voice sounded thin, as though it belonged to somebody else. The judge turned, eyebrows raised. Imani drew a breath, took a step towards the table, and reached for the corner of the cloth.
Behind her, the brass band launched into a march, bright and oblivious. Nobody seemed to notice that, inside the tent, the applause had died away.

title: The Scruff on the Chart
text: In the summer of 1967, a young research student named Jocelyn Bell was working at Cambridge University on an unusual scientific instrument. It was a radio telescope, yet it bore no resemblance to the gleaming domes that most people imagine: it was a vast field of wooden posts, strung with miles of wire, which Bell and her fellow students had helped to construct by hammering in the posts and stretching out the cable by hand.

The telescope did not take photographs. Instead, it detected radio waves arriving from space, and a pen recorded them as a wavering line on a moving roll of paper. Every day the pen produced about thirty metres of chart, and somebody had to examine every centimetre of it. That responsibility fell to Bell, who worked through the endless paper with a ruler, a pencil and a formidable amount of patience.

A few weeks into the survey, she noticed something peculiar. Among the jagged lines lay a small, untidy mark, which she later described as “a bit of scruff”. Most observers would have dismissed it, since radio telescopes pick up all manner of interference and scruff was common. Bell, however, remembered having seen the same mark before, in exactly the same place, and she turned back through her earlier charts to confirm it.

This was puzzling. Interference from cars and machinery ordinarily followed the human day, but this mark appeared at the same point in the sky each time, keeping to the stars rather than the clock. Bell asked for the signal to be recorded at a much faster speed. When the new chart came back, the scruff had been stretched into a neat row of pulses, each arriving a little more than a second after the last.

No natural signal had ever been known to keep time like a clock. For a brief spell, the team wondered, only half seriously, whether they might be receiving a message, and they jokingly labelled the source LGM-1, short for “Little Green Men”. But when Bell discovered a second signal, then a third and a fourth, in different regions of the sky, the theory collapsed. It seemed absurd that several distant civilisations should all be “speaking” in precisely the same rhythm. The pulses had to come from something natural.

The sources became known as pulsars. A pulsar is a tiny, rapidly spinning star, left behind when a much larger star has exhausted its fuel and collapsed. As it spins, it emits a beam of radio waves, rather like a lamp turning on a stand, and each time the beam sweeps across the Earth, a telescope registers a pulse.

In 1974, a Nobel Prize was awarded for the discovery, but it went to Bell’s supervisor rather than to her. Many scientists thought this unfair, yet Bell responded with remarkable composure. Decades afterwards, when she received a large prize of her own, she donated all of the money to support students who are under-represented in physics.

Her story is frequently told to remind young scientists that discoveries do not always announce themselves with a bang. Sometimes they arrive as a smudge on a page, waiting patiently for the person willing to notice.

title: The Stumble That Learned to Dance
text: In Bonwire, the mornings began with the sound of looms, a steady clack and thump that rolled from doorway to doorway like a drum passed along a street. Abena had grown up inside that rhythm and, much as with her own heartbeat, she had long since ceased to be aware of it.

Today she noticed everything, because her grandfather had stepped away from his loom and nodded towards the stool. “The final strip,” he said. Twenty-three narrow bands of cloth lay folded over the rail, each no wider than her hand and each patterned in gold, green and red; when the twenty-fourth was complete, they would be stitched edge to edge into a single cloth, made for a ceremony in the next town.

Abena sat, and as she pressed the pedals the threads rose and fell while the shuttle skipped between them with a soft whisper. For an hour all went well, until she glanced down at the pattern and her heart sank, for in her eagerness she had woven the zigzag one row too early, and it would now sit crooked against the strip beside it. The flaw was tiny, scarcely larger than a fingernail, but to her it glared like a drop of ink spilled across a clean white page.

She looked towards the doorway, where her grandfather was deep in conversation with a neighbour, his back turned. She could unpick the rows in secret, although that would take hours and the cloth was needed by Friday; alternatively, she could say nothing. “Nobody will notice one row,” she muttered, yet she remembered how her grandfather lifted each finished strip to the light and turned it slowly, as though he were reading it.

“Every strip has a name,” he had told her once. “The name is in the pattern, but the pattern is in the hands. Hurry, and the cloth remembers.” She had laughed at the time, since it had seemed a peculiar thing to say about cloth.
She was still staring at the fault when a shadow fell across the loom, and her grandfather bent close and studied the strip in a prolonged silence, until she could barely breathe.
“I am sorry,” she whispered. “I hurried.”

“Yes,” he said. “I can see where.” Then, to her astonishment, he smiled. “Do not unpick it. Look.” Taking the shuttle, he demonstrated how the following rows could climb from the stray zigzag, step by step, until the error became the first stair of an entirely new pattern. “In my father’s day we called this one ‘the stumble that learned to dance’. Some of the finest designs began as mistakes. But you must be brave enough to follow them.”

By evening the strip was finished, and the crooked little step sat at its centre, not concealed at all but woven into the design as though it had always been intended. On Friday the twenty-four strips were sewn together, and the cloth was carried away, gleaming like a river at sunset.

Nobody in the next town would ever discover which strip was Abena’s, but she would know, and so would her grandfather. And when the looms began again the following morning, clacking their old, patient rhythm, Abena found that she was listening.

title: Rivers of Ice
text: Mountain valleys come in two distinct shapes. Those cut by rivers are narrow and steep-sided, with a cross-section like the letter V. Others, however, are broad and flat-bottomed, with towering walls that rise almost vertically on either side, forming a shape closer to a U. Geologists have long known that the U-shaped valleys were not made by water at all. They were carved by glaciers.

A glacier begins high in the mountains, in places where more snow falls in winter than melts in summer. Year after year, fresh snow buries the older layers, and the enormous weight squeezes the lower snow until it is compressed into dense, solid ice. Eventually the mass becomes so heavy that it starts to creep downhill under its own weight. Although a glacier looks motionless, it may travel anything from a few centimetres to several metres in a single day.

As the ice advances, it shapes the landscape in two main ways. The first is plucking. Meltwater seeps into cracks in the bedrock and freezes, gripping fragments of stone. When the glacier moves on, it drags these rocks away, rather as a tooth might be pulled from a jaw. The second is abrasion. Stones frozen into the base and sides of the glacier scrape against the rock beneath like sandpaper, grinding it smooth and leaving long scratches, known as striations, which point in the direction the ice was travelling.

A river winds around obstacles, cutting mainly downwards, which is why river valleys are narrow. A glacier, by contrast, is a single vast slab that cannot bend easily. It ploughs straight through, scouring the floor and the sides equally, and so it widens and deepens the valley into a smooth trough. When the ice finally melts, that trough is left behind.

The retreating ice leaves other clues. High on the mountainsides, the source of a glacier often carves a rounded, armchair-shaped hollow called a cirque, and where two neighbouring cirques cut back towards each other, only a thin, jagged ridge remains between them. Smaller glaciers that fed into the main one were less powerful, so their valleys were not cut as deeply. When the ice vanished, these side valleys were left hanging high above the main trough, and streams now tumble from them as waterfalls.

Glaciers also act as conveyor belts. The rubble they collect is carried along, then dumped when the ice melts, forming ridges and mounds of mixed clay, sand and boulders called moraines. Some huge boulders, known as erratics, are deposited far from the rock they came from, and geologists can sometimes trace them back to their origin.

Much of Britain was once covered by thick ice, and its mountain landscapes still bear the signs. Anyone who walks into a broad, steep-walled valley with a waterfall spilling from a ledge high above is, in effect, standing inside the footprint of a vanished river of ice.

title: Miles of Stone
text: We began at Housesteads Roman Fort at nine o’clock, in a fine drizzle that could not decide whether it was rain or mist. My brother Kwesi had spent the entire car journey complaining that a wall was only a wall, while I had spent it reading aloud from the guidebook. Hadrian’s Wall, I had learned, stretches for about seventy-three miles across the north of England, from near Newcastle in the east to the shores of the Solway Firth in the west, and its construction began in AD 122 on the orders of the Emperor Hadrian.
“Seventy-three miles,” Kwesi had muttered. “By hand?”
“By soldiers,” I had replied. It was not much of an answer, but we were about to discover exactly how much it was worth.

Beyond the fort, the path climbed a grassy ridge, and there, quite suddenly, the wall was in front of us. It was not as tall as I had imagined; in places it rose no higher than my waist, and its grey stones were freckled with orange lichen. Yet it went on and on, rising and falling with the crags like the spine of some enormous sleeping animal, until the mist swallowed it. To the north, the ground fell away in a sheer cliff, and I could see why the builders had chosen this line, since any enemy would have had to climb the whole way in full view.

Roughly every mile, we passed the remains of a small square building set into the wall, with a gateway through its middle. These were milecastles, where soldiers once stood guard. The guidebook explained that our word “mile” derives from the Latin for a thousand paces, because Roman soldiers measured distance by counting their steps. When I read this out, Kwesi pretended not to be listening, although I noticed that he had begun to count his own.

By late morning the wind had scoured the mist away, and the whole country opened out below us: green hills, tiny farms, sheep dotted about like scattered rice, and a dark lake glittering beneath the crags. I knelt beside the wall and laid my palm against a stone. It was cold and rough, and it had been cut, shaped and hauled into place by somebody almost two thousand years ago, an effort that I found quite impossible to picture.
Kwesi had at last stopped complaining, and he was standing a little way off, hands buried in his pockets, gazing north across the desolate, empty land, apparently with nothing whatsoever to say.
“What would it have been like,” he asked at last, “to stand here and look at that, every day?”

I could not answer. I thought of all the soldiers who must have stood on this ridge, far from home, watching for something that might never come, and of the wind, which surely blew as hard for them as it did for us.

By the time we turned back, my feet ached and my hair was plastered flat with drizzle. But when I glanced behind me, the wall lay across the hills like a grey thread, stitched through the landscape by careful hands, and it seemed to me that it was no longer only a wall.

title: After the Final Whistle
text: An hour after the final whistle, the stadium had surrendered its roar. The crowds, who had poured through the turnstiles in noisy tributaries, had drained away into the darkening streets, and what remained was a vast concave silence, as though the whole structure were holding its breath. Floodlights still burned on their tall masts, but they had been dimmed to a tired amber, and the pitch beneath them glowed an almost unnatural green.

In the stands, the emptiness felt strangely full. Thousands of plastic seats climbed away in curving terraces, their bright colours drained to grey by the fading light, and each one seemed to hold the memory of somebody who had leapt from it. Scarves had been left draped over railings, a single glove lay abandoned on a step, and a trodden programme fluttered along the concrete like a wounded bird. Everywhere the air smelled of cold chips, wet grass and spilled tea.

Down on the touchline, a small band of workers moved patiently through the litter. They wore orange jackets that glowed in the gloom, and they pushed wide brooms in slow, steady sweeps, gathering a drift of wrappers, paper cups and confetti into heaps. Their voices carried oddly in the cavernous space, rising to the roof and returning a moment late, so that every casual remark seemed to be spoken twice.

Beneath the stands, the players’ tunnel yawned like the mouth of a cave. Its walls were lined with faded photographs, and a puddle of muddy water had gathered at the foot of the steps, marking the place where, only an hour earlier, two teams had waited shoulder to shoulder for the signal to run out into the light. Nobody stood there now, although somewhere within, a door creaked as it swung slowly shut on its hinges.

The pitch itself bore the marks of the evening. Long scuffs curved across the penalty area where boots had skidded, and in the centre circle the turf was churned to bare brown earth. A groundsman knelt with a small fork, pressing the torn divots back into place, one at a time, as gently as if he were tucking a child into bed. By morning, he explained, the damage would be barely visible.

Above the far goal, the great scoreboard still showed the result, its white letters blazing on black. Nobody had thought to switch it off. It seemed to shine for an audience that had already gone home, insisting on a moment that was over.

Then, one by one, the floodlights were extinguished. Darkness poured down from the rim of the roof, swallowing the seats, the touchline and finally the pitch. For a heartbeat the scoreboard glowed alone, and then it, too, went out. All that remained was the distant hum of the city beyond the walls, and the quiet ticking of cooling metal as the stadium settled down to wait for the next time it would be needed.

title: The Height Marks
text: On the last evening, the house had already begun to forget them, its rooms, stripped of rugs and pictures, returning every footstep as an echo. Pale rectangles on the walls marked the places where eleven years of family life had hung until that morning. Amara drifted from room to room with her hands buried in her pockets, like a visitor who had wandered in by mistake and was trying to decide whom she ought to apologise to.

In the hall, removal boxes stood stacked like a small cardboard town. Her father was wrapping the last of the glasses in newspaper, humming tunelessly, while her mother, telephone pressed to her ear, kept up the bright, brisk voice that she reserved for difficult days, saying “yes” and “no” and “we’ll manage”. Nobody noticed when Amara slipped upstairs.

The landing bulb had been packed away with everything else, so she climbed by the glow of the street lamp, which laid a long amber oblong across the floorboards. In her old bedroom she knelt beside the door frame, where pencil lines climbed the wood in uneven steps, each one labelled in her father’s slanting hand with a date and a name: “Amara, age 4”; “Amara, age 7, standing on tiptoe (disqualified)”. Together they rose like a slow, stubborn staircase, the newest sitting just above her shoulder.

Until tonight she had regarded them as a nuisance. Every birthday had brought the same ritual: the flattened book on her head, the pencil and the groan. Now, in the half-light, they seemed less like measurements than like a diary composed in a language that only the door could read.

“We can’t take the door,” said a voice behind her. Her father stood in the doorway with a glass still wrapped in newsprint, and although he spoke lightly, he did not quite meet her eye. “The new people will paint over it, I expect. That’s what people do.”

“I know,” said Amara, who did not add that painting over something seemed a curious way of announcing that it had never mattered. Her father crouched beside her, his knees clicking, and studied the lowest mark, the one barely a hand above the skirting board. “You were so small,” he murmured, and his voice snagged in the middle, like a sleeve catching on a nail.

Then he drew the pencil from behind his ear but, instead of adding a line, pressed the flat of his hand to the wood just above the highest mark and held it there, as though he were trying to warm it. “Let them paint,” he said gruffly. “It will have to go through a great deal of paint to get to that.”

Amara understood, without being able to explain how, that he was not really talking about the door. She laid her palm beside his; the wood was cool and slightly rough, and the two hands, one broad and one narrow, covered almost the same patch of shadow. Downstairs, her mother had stopped talking, and in the sudden hush the empty house seemed to be listening, so that for the first time all day it no longer sounded like a place that had forgotten anything.

title: Give Us Back the Night
text: Step outside on a clear night in almost any town and look up. What greets you is not the sky our ancestors knew, a crowded, glittering river of stars that seemed to pour from one horizon to the other, but a dull orange-grey haze in which a few stubborn survivors are pinned. Scientists estimate that more than a third of the world’s population can no longer see the Milky Way from where they live. We have illuminated our streets so lavishly that we have, without ever quite intending to, switched off the heavens.

The consequences reach well beyond the loss of scenery. Living things have spent millions of years arranging their lives around the alternation of light and dark, and artificial glare throws that arrangement into confusion. Migrating birds, many of which travel at night and steer partly by the stars, can be lured off course by brightly lit buildings and may circle them until they are exhausted. Newly hatched sea turtles crawl towards the brightest horizon, which for countless generations meant the moonlit sea; beside a lit hotel, it can mean precisely the wrong direction. Even the humble moth, battering itself against a porch lamp, is squandering energy it needs to feed and find a mate.

Nor are people exempt. Our bodies interpret darkness as the signal to rest, and bedrooms flooded with light from outside may make it harder to sleep soundly. Then there is the matter of wonder. Generation after generation has gazed at the night sky and asked how vast the universe might be and where humanity fits within it, and a child who has never glimpsed the stars has been quietly denied the opportunity to ask.

Some will object that we cannot return to candles, and they are right, but nobody is proposing that we should. The difficulty is seldom too much lighting; it is careless lighting. A lamp that shines upwards, or sideways into a bedroom window, illuminates nothing that needs illuminating, whereas fittings that direct their beams downwards, towards the pavement, do the job and leave the sky alone. Warmer-coloured bulbs, reduced brightness after midnight and sensors that switch lights off when nobody is about are inexpensive, ordinary and effective, and they save money too, because energy that is not wasted need not be paid for.

Others fear that darker streets are less safe. Yet the evidence for this is weaker than most of us assume. What matters for safety is light that is well aimed rather than merely plentiful, and dazzling glare can in fact make it harder for our eyes to pick out what lies in the shadows.

Some places have already shown the way. Communities around the world have earned official recognition as dark-sky places by replacing their lamps and asking residents to switch off unnecessary lights, and visitors now travel long distances simply to lie on the grass and look up. If they can manage it, so can the rest of us. The stars have not gone anywhere; we have merely hidden them, and what we have hidden we are perfectly able to uncover. All that is required is the modest, sensible decision to light what we need and to leave the remainder to the night.

title: Saturdays at Mr Iqbal’s
text: The summer I turned eleven, my mother, weary of finding me indoors with the curtains half drawn, arranged for me to spend my Saturdays at Mr Iqbal’s bookbinding workshop above the launderette on Fenner Street. I went reluctantly, picturing a dusty room and a dull old man, and I resolved to be bored with as much dignity as I could manage.

The workshop dismantled that resolution within minutes. It smelt of warm glue, leather and something sharp and green that I later discovered was paste, and every surface bore evidence of work in progress: presses with great iron screws, spools of waxed thread, and heaps of loose pages tied in bundles like sheaves of corn. Mr Iqbal himself was small and precise, with half-moon glasses and a habit of humming whenever he concentrated, and he regarded me not as a nuisance but as though I were a book whose binding he could not yet judge.

“Sit,” he said, handing me a battered paperback that had come apart at its spine. “Tell me what is wrong with it.” I said that the pages had fallen out. He waited. I said that the glue had failed. He waited longer. Eventually, by a process of elimination that felt like being slowly cornered, I noticed that the thread had rotted and that the cover had been forced to do a job it was never meant to do. “Good,” said Mr Iqbal, and that single word gave me more satisfaction than any prize I had ever been handed at school.

For weeks I did nothing but sew: needle through the fold, out, round and back, pulled tight, but never so tight that the paper puckered, and never so loose that the book would sag. My first attempts looked like something a cat had chewed. Mr Iqbal never criticised; he would simply cut my stitches with a little curved blade and say, “Again.” I came to dread that word, and then, without noticing the moment the change occurred, I began to hear it differently, less as a verdict than as an invitation.

In August, a woman brought in a family Bible whose spine was crumbling and whose pages had grown soft as cloth. Mr Iqbal let me hold it while he explained what he intended to do, and I noticed that he handled it the way one carries a brimming cup. “It is not our job to make it look new,” he said. “It is our job to make it able to go on.” I have pondered that sentence more often than any lesson I was ever formally taught.

On the last Saturday of the holidays, he presented me with a small notebook bound in dark blue cloth, its stitches so even that I hardly recognised them as mine until I spotted the tiny crooked knot at the base of the spine. “I left your knot in,” he said, “so that you will always know who made it.” I never told him that I had meant to thank him all summer, and that when the moment arrived the words simply would not bind. Yet I have kept that notebook for over thirty years, and it has never once come apart.

title: How a Seed Knows When to Sprout
text: A seed is a plant waiting for its moment. Inside its hard outer coat lies a tiny embryo, packed with just enough stored food to begin growing, and it is in a state scientists call dormancy: alive, but almost entirely inactive. Dormancy is not laziness. It is a survival strategy, because a seed that sprouts at the wrong time, on a warm afternoon in midwinter, for instance, would be killed by the next frost. So how does a seed know when the time is right?

The first signal is nearly always water. A dry seed contains very little moisture, and until it takes some in, its chemistry cannot get going. When rain soaks the soil, the seed swells as it absorbs water, and its coat may crack. The moisture wakes up chemicals, called enzymes, that begin to turn stored food into energy. However, water alone is not enough. Most seeds also need oxygen, because they release energy from food in a process similar to breathing, and a suitable temperature, which is why seeds planted in cold ground often sit quietly until spring.

Many species add extra conditions to make certain. Some seeds from cold regions will not sprout until they have spent several weeks in the cold, and so they are protected from germinating during a mild spell in autumn. Some seeds have coats so tough that they must be worn thin, by rubbing against stones, by soaking, or by passing through the digestive system of a bird, before water can get in. Tiny seeds, which hold little food, often need light, a sign that they lie near enough to the surface for their first leaves to reach the sun. In parts of the world where wildfires are common, certain seeds wait for the chemicals in smoke.

Once every condition is met, the seed acts fast. The first part to emerge is the root, which anchors the seedling and starts to draw water from the soil. Next, a shoot pushes upwards, bending towards the light. Until its leaves open and begin making food from sunlight, the young plant survives entirely on the supplies that the seed provided.

This careful timing matters because a seed has only one chance. Sprouting is a gamble: a seed that commits too early risks frost or drought, while one that waits too long may be shaded out by neighbours that are already growing. Seeds therefore behave like cautious investors, spending their single store of energy only when the odds look favourable.

Some seeds can wait for astonishingly long. A date palm seed found in an ancient fortress in Israel was about two thousand years old when scientists planted it, and it sprouted. Not every seed is so patient, and many die if their conditions are never right, but this remarkable ability to pause, and then to respond at precisely the right instant, is one reason plants have spread to almost every corner of the planet.

title: Platform Four, Before Dawn
text: At half past four, the station belongs to no one. The great iron roof, blackened by a century of steam and smoke, arches overhead like the ribs of some enormous sleeping creature, and beneath it the platforms stretch away into a darkness that the tired lamps do little more than dent. Every sound is magnified: a dropped coin rings like a bell, and when a distant door slams, the echo takes a long time to die.

The air is cold and faintly metallic, tasting of rails and rain. A pigeon shuffles along a girder, ruffling itself into a small grey cushion, and far below it a cleaner in a yellow jacket pushes a wide broom in slow, unhurried arcs, gathering up the remains of yesterday: ticket stubs, sweet wrappers, a single glove. He hums as he works, and the tune, stripped of its words by distance, could belong to any country.

Gradually, the platform acquires its people, one at a time, like ink spreading in water. A man in a suit that looks slept in stands with his eyes closed, clutching a briefcase against his chest as if it were a shield, while on a bench nearby a girl with a cello case almost as tall as herself watches the departure board with the solemn patience of the very young, her feet not quite touching the ground. An elderly couple share a flask, passing the cup between them without a word, in the manner of people who said all the important things many years ago.

Then the board flickers. Letters shuffle, rattle and settle, and every head lifts at once, like a field of flowers turning to a change in the light. Somewhere beyond the buffers the rails begin to sing, a thin, rising note that swells until it fills the whole cavernous space, and two round lamps swim out of the gloom as the train arrives slowly, exhaling clouds of white breath, its windows glowing like a row of small, warm rooms.

Doors clunk open. The man with the briefcase steps aboard first, without a backward glance. The girl hauls her cello after her, with help from the cleaner, who lifts it as gently as a sleeping child and receives a solemn nod in return. The old couple linger at the door, he tucking the flask into her bag, she straightening his collar although it does not need it, and then they, too, are gone, and the train, after a pause that feels a little too long, gathers itself and slides away.

The lamps seem brighter when it has gone. The pigeon hops down to inspect the glove. Along the eastern end of the platform the darkness has thinned to the colour of weak tea, and the first pale light slants beneath the roof, gilding the dust that hangs in the air, while the cleaner leans on his broom and watches the empty rails shine, as if they were still holding something.

title: Ada and the Thinking Machine
text: In 1815, in London, a baby girl called Augusta Ada Byron was born. Her father was Lord Byron, a famous poet, but he left England when Ada was only a few months old, and she hardly knew him. Her mother, Annabella, who brought her up, wanted Ada’s education to be very different from her father’s, so Ada learned logic, mathematics and science, and not only poetry.

Ada had private tutors, and she was good with numbers and even better with ideas. As a child, she wrote about a machine that could carry a person through the air, and she studied how birds’ bodies were made in order to work out how wings might be built. She never built the machine, but the idea shows how her mind worked. To Ada, something that looked impossible was a puzzle to solve, not a wall to stop at.

When she was seventeen, Ada met Charles Babbage, a mathematician and inventor who was designing machines to do sums. His first design, called the Difference Engine, was meant to make tables of numbers without mistakes, because tables copied out by hand were often full of errors. Later he planned something much more daring, the Analytical Engine, which could be given a list of instructions and follow them, so that it could be used for many kinds of problem, not just one. Ada was fascinated, and the two became friends and wrote to each other for many years.

In 1842, an Italian engineer named Luigi Menabrea wrote an article in French about the Analytical Engine. Ada was asked to translate it into English, but she did much more than that, adding notes of her own that grew to about three times the length of the article. In them she showed, step by step, how the engine could be told to work out a list of numbers. Many people today call this the first computer program, although the machine was never finished, so the program was never run.

Ada’s best idea was not about sums at all, because she saw that the engine might work with symbols as well as numbers. If the rules of music could be written down using symbols, she said, the machine might one day make music of its own. At that time, people thought of such machines as clever adding tools, so this was a huge leap. She also took care to point out that the machine could only do what people told it to do and could not think up anything new by itself. People still talk about this warning today.

Ada’s notes were printed in 1843 with only her initials, A.A.L., on them. For many years afterwards, they were largely overlooked. Then, in the twentieth century, real computers were built, and people found out how much Ada had seen ahead of her time. Today a computer language is named after her, and every October there is a day to celebrate her work. She was not a builder of machines; she was something rarer: a person who saw, before the machines existed, what they might become.
